title: You Want Your Children to Love Jesus—But They’re Learning Christianity by Watching You
paragraphs: You Want Your Children to Love Jesus—But They’re Learning Christianity by Watching You

Your children may forget some of the family devotions you led. But they may remember for the rest of their lives what your Christianity looked like when you were angry, embarrassed, exhausted, offended, disappointed, or wrong.
There is a frightening possibility that almost no Christian parent wants to consider.
You can teach your children the right Bible stories and still teach them the wrong picture of Christianity.
You can bring them to church.
You can pray before meals.
You can put Scripture on the wall.

You can tell them that Jesus forgives sinners, that God answers prayer, that Christians should love their enemies, that money is not everything, that forgiveness matters, that holiness matters, that eternity matters.
And then they watch you.
That is where the lesson becomes real.
They watch what happens when someone humiliates you.
They hear how you speak about people when those people leave the room.
They notice whether the stranger gets Christian kindness while your spouse gets Christian leftovers.
They notice whether you can admit that you were wrong.
They notice whether “I’m sorry” exists in your vocabulary without a “but” attached to it.
They notice what happens when money gets tight.
They notice what happens when prayers seem unanswered.
They notice whether Sunday changes Monday.
And somewhere in those ordinary moments, your children are assembling an answer to a question they may never say aloud:
Is this Jesus my parents talk about actually real enough to change a human being?
That question should bring every Christian parent and grandparent to their knees.
Not because faithful parenting requires perfection.
It doesn’t.
If perfection were the requirement, none of us could disciple anyone.
The Gospel itself begins with the devastating truth that we are sinners who need mercy. Our children do not need parents pretending they have never failed.
They need to see what a sinner looks like when Jesus Christ is actually Lord.
Moses gave Israel a command that generations of believing parents have treasured:

“Thou shalt love the LORD thy God with all thine heart, and with all thy soul, and with all thy might. And these words, which I command thee this day, shall be in thine heart: And thou shalt teach them diligently unto thy children, and shalt talk of them when thou sittest in thine house, and when thou walkest by the way, and when thou liest down, and when thou risest up.”
Deuteronomy 6:5–7, KJV.
The Hebrew makes the order difficult to ignore.

וְאָהַבְתָּ אֵת יְהוָה אֱלֹהֶיךָ
בְּכָל־לְבָבְךָ וּבְכָל־נַפְשְׁךָ וּבְכָל־מְאֹדֶךָ
Ve’ahavta et-YHWH Elohekha, bekhol-levavkha uvekhol-nafshekha uvekhol-me’odekha.
“And you shall love the LORD your God with all your heart, and with all your soul, and with all your might.”
Then comes something crucial:
וְהָיוּ הַדְּבָרִים הָאֵלֶּה ... עַל־לְבָבֶךָ
Vehayu haddevarim ha’elleh ... al-levavekha.
“These words ... shall be upon your heart.”
Upon your heart.
Before the words are diligently impressed upon the children, they are to live in the parent.

That does not mean parents earn their children’s salvation through exemplary behavior. They cannot. Salvation belongs to the Lord, and no amount of flawless parenting can regenerate another human heart.
It means biblical instruction was never intended to be merely information transferred from an adult mouth into a child’s brain.
God’s truth is meant to possess us.
And then, from a life possessed by that truth, we speak of Him.
At home.
On the road.
At bedtime.
In the morning.
In ordinary life.
Your kitchen becomes part of the classroom.
Your car becomes part of the classroom.
Your bank account becomes part of the classroom.
Your marriage becomes part of the classroom.
Your disappointments become part of the classroom.
Your repentance becomes part of the classroom.
Even the way you respond after losing your temper becomes part of the classroom.
And maybe that last one is where someone reading this already feels the ache.
Because you remember yesterday.
You remember what you said.
Maybe you saw your child’s face change when your voice changed.
Maybe you slammed something.
Maybe you insulted your spouse within earshot of them.
Maybe you humiliated your child and called it discipline.
Maybe you demanded respect while behaving disrespectfully.
Maybe you spent the whole drive to church tearing somebody apart and then walked through the church doors smiling.
Maybe you have been teaching your children about grace while making your home a place where nobody is allowed to fail.
Maybe your children know that Jesus forgives because their Sunday school teacher told them.
But they do not know what forgiveness feels like because resentment has been living at your dinner table for years.
That hurts.
But conviction is not the same thing as condemnation.
For those who are in Christ Jesus, failure does not have to become the final chapter.
This is where the Gospel enters the house.
Not as decoration.
Not as a slogan.
Not as religious damage control.
As resurrection.
Your children do not need you to manufacture an image of Christian perfection.
They need to see repentance.
Imagine what happens when a father who has sinned against his child walks into the bedroom, sits beside the bed, looks that child in the eyes and says:
“I was wrong.”
No excuse.
No blame shifting.
No “You made me angry.”
No lecture disguised as an apology.
“I sinned against you. What I said was wrong. Jesus does not excuse my sin, and neither should I. Will you forgive me?”
Something enormous has just happened.
The father has not lost spiritual authority by repenting.
He has demonstrated where Christian authority comes from.
Not ego.
Not domination.
Not pretending.
Christ.
The child has just watched Christianity move from theory into flesh and blood.
They have learned that Daddy needs grace too.
That Mommy needs Jesus too.
That adults do not graduate from repentance.
That the Cross is not merely where bad people become Christians; it remains the place where Christians remember that our only boast is Christ.
Your children may someday forget the exact sermon you discussed over Sunday lunch.
They may never forget hearing you say:
“Please forgive me.”
They may forget the devotional book you used when they were eight.
They may remember watching you forgive someone who wounded you.
They may forget a hundred lessons about trusting God.
They may remember the month when money disappeared and fear entered the house—and still they watched you pray rather than worship panic.
They may forget your lecture about loving your neighbor.
They may remember how you treated the waitress who got your order wrong.
They may forget your warnings about worldly materialism.
They may remember whether possessions controlled your mood.
They may forget your explanation of Christian marriage.
They may remember how you spoke to their mother.
How you spoke to their father.
How affection looked.
How conflict looked.
How forgiveness looked.
Children are watching what Christianity does to us when Christianity costs something.
That is often where faith becomes credible.

Jesus Himself warned against a religion concerned with outward appearance while the inner life remains corrupt. His fiercest rebukes were not aimed at broken people who knew they needed mercy, but repeatedly at religious hypocrisy that performed righteousness before others while resisting the deeper reality of God’s rule.
Your home is one of the hardest places to maintain a religious performance.
Eventually the costume slips.
And maybe that is mercy.
Because perhaps the greatest spiritual gift you can give your children is not the illusion that their parent has everything together.
Perhaps it is allowing them to watch Jesus Christ deal honestly with the person you actually are.
Let them see you open the Bible because you are hungry for God, not merely because you want them to become religious.
Let them hear you pray when there is no audience.
Let them watch you give when nobody applauds.
Let them hear you refuse gossip.
Let them see you shut your mouth when your flesh desperately wants the last word.
Let them watch you honor people who cannot advance your career.
Let them see you treat cleaners, servers, laborers, drivers, employees, strangers, relatives, and difficult people as human beings bearing dignity before God.
Let them discover that your Christianity survives inconvenience.
Let them see you suffer.
This may be one of the hardest lessons of all.
Because eventually life will wound you in front of them.
A diagnosis may come.
Someone may die.
A business may collapse.
A friendship may betray you.
A prayer may appear unanswered.
The future you imagined may disappear.
And your children will watch.
They do not need to see a parent who never cries.
Jesus wept.
They do not need to see someone who pretends suffering does not hurt.
Biblical faith is not emotional anesthesia.
They need to see where you run when it hurts.
There is a difference between saying, “Christ is enough,” when everything is comfortable and whispering His name through tears when something you loved has been buried.
A child who sees that may someday remember it in a hospital corridor of their own.
Years from now, when their world is falling apart, perhaps they will remember:
I watched Mom suffer, and she still ran to Jesus.
I watched Dad break, and somehow Christ held him.
That memory can become a witness.
But parents also need to hear something equally important.
You cannot save your children.
You can teach.
You can pray.
You can model repentance.
You can discipline lovingly.
You can saturate your home with Scripture.
You can confess your hypocrisy.
You can ask forgiveness.
You can speak the Gospel faithfully.
But you cannot regenerate their hearts.
Only God can give life.
That truth should humble us, but it should also relieve us from the crushing fantasy that one parenting mistake automatically writes the ending of our children’s story.
Some parents are reading this with adult children who have walked away from Christianity.
And your heart is already accusing you.
You are replaying everything.
Every argument.
Every missed opportunity.
Every inconsistency.
Every moment when your children saw something in you that contradicted what you claimed to believe.
Where repentance is needed, repent.
If an apology is owed, give it.
Even if your child is thirty-five.
Even if the conversation is awkward.
Even if admitting your failure bruises your pride.
You can say:
“I realize there were times when the Christianity I showed you did not look much like Jesus. I cannot undo those moments. I was wrong. I am sorry. Please forgive me.”
But after genuine repentance, do not pretend you are sovereign over another person's soul.
Your failure is real.
Christ's grace is greater.
Peter failed spectacularly.
He denied Jesus.
Not privately.
Not ambiguously.
Three times.
Yet Jesus did not write Peter’s obituary at the fire where Peter failed.
After the resurrection, Christ restored him.
That is the heartbeat of everything Gospel Warrior exists to proclaim:
Your worst parenting moment does not need to become your final parenting moment.
Your family may have chapters you wish had never been written.
Alcohol.
Anger.
Infidelity.
Divorce.
Absence.
Pride.
Harshness.
Materialism.
Pornography.
Bitterness.
Neglect.
Religious hypocrisy.
Years when everyone looked fine in photographs while the house was quietly bleeding.
The Gospel does not require you to rename darkness as light.
It calls you to bring darkness into the light.
“For all have sinned, and come short of the glory of God.”
Romans 3:23.
That includes parents.
And grandparents.
Pastors.
Sunday school teachers.
The people posting Bible verses.
The people writing Christian articles.
Every one of us.
But Scripture does not end at Romans 3:23.
We are “justified freely by his grace through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus” (Romans 3:24).
That is Christianity.
Not good parents rescuing bad children.
Not respectable families proving themselves better than broken families.
Sinners being rescued by Jesus Christ.
Your children need more than your example.
They need Christ.
They need the Son of God who lived the righteousness we could not live, bore sin at the Cross, died, was buried, and rose again.
They need to know repentance is not merely feeling guilty.
It is turning toward God.
They need to know grace is not God pretending sin does not matter.
Grace cost blood.
They need to know forgiveness is not cheap.
Christ was crucified.
They need to know Christianity is not primarily “become a nicer person.”
It is reconciliation with God through Jesus Christ and a transformed life flowing from union with Him.
And perhaps one of the clearest ways they will begin to understand that is by watching grace transform you.
So tonight, before correcting your children again, ask Christ to search you.
What are they learning by watching me?
What does my anger teach them about Jesus?
What does my marriage teach them?
What does my phone use teach them?
What does my spending teach them?
What does my private life teach them?
What does my speech teach them?
What does the way I treat people who cannot benefit me teach them?
What does my reaction when I am corrected teach them?
What does my repentance teach them?
Not because your performance can save them.
Because your life should not continually contradict the Savior you are asking them to trust.
Go to Jesus.
Then, where necessary, go to your child.
Maybe tonight the most powerful family devotion will not begin with you telling your children what they did wrong.
Maybe it begins with:
“Dad needs to apologize.”
“Mom was wrong.”
“I have not shown you Christ well in this area.”
“Will you forgive me?”
And then pray together.
There are children who have heard thousands of Christian words but have rarely watched an adult genuinely repent.
Change that.
You do not need to explain everything publicly. But sometimes one honest sentence is enough to remind another exhausted parent that they are not the only one fighting for their family on their knees.
And parents, grandparents, pastors, teachers—share this.
Not because sharing a Facebook article earns favor with God. It does not.
It does not.
We are saved by grace, through faith, and our boasting belongs in Christ, not ourselves.
Send it privately to a grandparent who has been praying for the next generation.
Save it too.
Because you may need these words again after a day when you do not parent the way you hoped you would.
It cannot purchase blessing, salvation, spiritual status, or His approval.
Jesus cannot be bought.
But supporting Gospel-centered work can be one practical expression of generosity when it is done freely, prayerfully, and for God's glory.
Look at the people God has placed in your home.
Remember that discipleship is happening in the ordinary moments.
Your children are listening when you pray.
But they are also listening when you are angry.
They are watching you worship.
But they are also watching you apologize.
They are hearing what you say about Jesus.
But they are also discovering what you really believe when life hurts.
You will fail.
When you do, do not teach them to hide.
Teach them where sinners go.
To Jesus.
Teach them that confession is not the death of a Christian testimony.
Sometimes it is where the testimony finally becomes believable.
Teach them that shame does not get the last word.
Teach them that a father can repent.
A mother can change.
A marriage can be healed.
A wounded family can begin again.
A prodigal can come home.
A hypocrite can step into the light.
A sinner can be forgiven.
Because the center of Christianity was never the perfection of your family.
It is the perfection of Christ.
And maybe, years from now, your children will not remember a parent who never failed.
Maybe they will remember something far more powerful:
They watched you fail—and then they watched you keep running back to Jesus.
And if this exposed something hidden in your own home, do not merely feel convicted.
Repent where repentance is needed.
Forgive where forgiveness is commanded.
Apologize where you have sinned.
And bring your family back to the feet of Christ.
Because someday your children may forget many of the words you taught them about Jesus—
but may God let them remember that whenever your life broke apart, they watched you crawl back to the Cross.
